# Ocean-going ships (carvel hull, sternpost rudder, mixed square and lateen rig) (`ship_design_caravel_carrack`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/navigation.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Navigation, transport & exploration (`navigation`)
- Deps: helped by wind_systems_ocean_currents
- Core idea: In 1490 Iberian pilots already use both caravels and larger cargo ships called naus or naos. A typical caravel used on the African coast has shallow draught and lateen sails, useful for exploring anchorages and working to windward by tacking. A square-rigged caravel can carry square canvas forward and a lateen aft. The larger carrack has capacity for stores and freight, usually with square sails on the fore and main masts and a lateen mizzen to help balance the helm. In a carvel hull the planks meet edge to edge. This describes the planking, while frame-first describes the order of construction. A sternpost rudder gives the helmsman control while water flows past it. On the 1492 voyage the Santa María is a nao, the Pinta and Niña caravels. Their size and rig have to be reconstructed from incomplete records.
- Pitfalls:
  - Thinking Columbus's ships were primitive or tiny for their task; Santa María, Pinta and Niña were working sailing vessels whose exact dimensions and carrying capacities are uncertain, and caravels were the explorers' choice
  - Saying sails let ships sail straight into the wind
  - Assuming ocean crossings require carvel planking; Norse clinker-built ships had crossed the North Atlantic centuries earlier
  - Overloading the castles; top weight reduces stability; flooding through open gunports contributed to the losses of Mary Rose in 1545 and Vasa in 1628
- History: china: Han period – stern-mounted steering oar or rudder on a Han pottery ship model; Song–Ming multi-masted junks with balanced rudders; islamic: from the 1st millennium AD – lateen-rigged sewn-plank dhows in the Indian Ocean; europe: c. 1180–1240 – sternpost rudder on northern cogs; 14th–15th c. three-masted carrack; c. 1440 Portuguese caravel for the Africa voyages; by 1500 the full-rigged ship; rome: 1st c. BC–4th c. AD – large mortise-and-tenon shell-built merchantmen; the shift to frame-first building is complete in the Mediterranean by c. 1000

  - Richard W. Unger, The Ship in the Medieval Economy, 600–1600 (1980)
  - Roger C. Smith, Vanguard of Empire: Ships of Exploration in the Age of Columbus (1993)
  - Lincoln P. Paine, The Sea and Civilization: A Maritime History of the World (2013)
